content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
__Summary.__ This paper proposes a framework for a more principled evaluation of unsupervised and self-supervised GNN embeddings. Their framework consists simply in applying a k-means clustering (based on the underlying known classes, although there is a  little bit of ambiguity in that regard, as highlighted by the reviewers) and characterise clustering in terms of the NMI, F1 score, modularity and conductance. The authors evaluate according to those metrics different methods.




__Summary of the reviews.__ The reviewers unequivocally advise a rejection of the paper. While the idea is not devoid of interest, there is no innovation in this paper: it is merely an evaluation of datasets based on clustering metrics. This submission is probably not suitable for ICLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the task of community detection in graphs. Specifically, it employs the K-means algorithm to partition the set of nodes into clusters -- each cluster being considered as a community. As vectors of node representations, the paper applies a range of different methods, such as DAEGC etc. The paper then presents a comparative analysis between these different node representation approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. Several node representation approaches were tested.
2. Experiments conducted over a large number of graph datasets.

Weaknesses:

1. Lack of novelty --- K-means clustering approaches have already been tried out.
2. Lack of baselines --- no comparisons with modularity-driven unsupervised approaches (which work fairly well).
3. No experiments on LFR networks (class of synthetically generated graphs commonly used to evaluate community detection algorithms).
4. It's not clear if the datasets used had ground-truth community information.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The novelty of the paper is limited (see weaknesses and the summary).
More clarity is needed about the existence of ground-truth information of the communities.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper addresses the task of community detection in graphs. Specifically, it employs the K-means algorithm to partition the set of nodes into clusters -- each cluster being considered as a community. As vectors of node representations, the paper applies a range of different methods, such as DAEGC etc. Most of these employ noise contrastive estimation. It is surprising to see why a simple noise contrastive estimation method, such as node2vec, wasn't used.

The research offers limited novelty. There have been papers that have applied K-means on different node embedding techniques, e.g., https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0167865521002324 and also end-to-end approaches for community detection https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3132847.3132925

What's also surprising to see is the non-existence of any baselines. What happens when standard modularity-based approaches or their extensions such as LPA, IMAP etc. are used?

It's not clear if the datasets that were used contained the ground-truth communities. There exists quite a few Stanford graph datasets with existing communities for the ground-truth, e.g., the DBLP, Youtube, Amazon product purchase networks etc. It is also crucial to report community detection experiments on different instances of the class of LFR networks (synthetically generated graphs specifically for the purpose of evaluating community detection).

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper discusses the misalignment issue on dataset, evaluation metric and hyperparameter tuning for GNN based community detection. Based on hyperparameter optimization (HPO), the authors build an evaluation environment for comparing different community detection based algorithms on different datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. The idea on standardize the evaluation procedure for community detection is good and could benefit the research community
2. The evaluation environment the authors build makes sense and could make fairer comparsion

Weaknesses
1. Majority of the content of this paper is on survey, which may not be suitable for ICLR
2. It is still not clear which evaluation metric to use. The authors use NMI for HPO, but it is still not clear if this is the best choice
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to read, but the quality is not good enough for an ICLR research paper. Reproducibility is hard with the current content.
content.summary_of_the_review: In general the idea of the paper is good and can benefit the research community. However, the content of this paper is not enough for a research paper and it is not strong enough to serve as a "standardization" for evaluation. I would encourage the authors to investigate more on this direction and polish the paper, but currently I recommend to reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a framework to evaluate unsupervised community detection using GNNs. In general, this framework can also be applied to other models. The framework separates the datasets into 80% for training and 20% for testing. Then, the training is separated into 80% for training and 20% for validation. Over the last two subsets, a search over multiple hyperparameters is applied to select the best of them based on some performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is easy to read, the problem is clearly motivated in the introduction. Also, the state of the art covers several papers of the last years. 

The evaluation process considered several databases, and interesting results are obtained. One little problem could be the size of the datasets, but this is a limitation of the GNN instead of a problem from the paper. 

However, the paper lacks novelty. The framework is not clearly described, or supported. It seems that the framework consists of the evaluation of four different measures. While their importance is explained vaguely, other measures are not even supported. Why should we use those measures (modularity and conductance)?

Also, the framework assumes that the right number of clusters is known from the beginning. So, the most basic part, the correct selection of the number of clusters is not even considered in this framework. Unfortunately, several of the new proposed GNN clustering models assume that the right number of clusters is known from the beginning, but this is not known in unsupervised datasets. So, if the framework wants to consider supervised metrics, then evaluate if the model is able to determine the right number of clusters too.

Finally, line 10 of the algorithm says: "if performance > best performance then"; however, best performance is not even defined. How do you calculate the best performance? Is it the average of the 4 measures? Is it a specific combination of them? 

Minor comments:

abstract: settings ,
Section 2.1: (2022) is survey of
Section 4.1: Also given is a set
Section 4.4: 200000 it should be 200,000
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
With respect to the clarity of the work. The paper is easy to read, the introduction motivates the problem. The state of art is extensive and covers several papers from last years. However, the main framework is not clearly stated. Reading the paper, it seems that the framework is the comparison of 4 different metrics over some test set. The main contribution must be highlighted. The results can also be improved. It is not clear the difference between the baseline hyperparameters versus the learned hyperparameters. Maybe you can create a second plot or add a second bar. Finally, explain the Tree Parzen_Estimator, it is important for your paper. 

The framework is not original. Most of the evaluation process is the minimum evaluation that you expect in a paper. Besides, there are several points that are not considered. Please see the weaknesses pointed out in the previous point.
content.summary_of_the_review: Considering that the main proposition is the use of 4 different metrics, the paper lacks novelty. Moreover, there is a very important assumption, that we know the real number of clusters before clustering the data. However, this information is not always available, and it is impossible to know the real number of clusters for unlabeled data. So, the proposed framework will be impossible to use.

content.title: A Framework for Comprehensive Evaluations of Graph Neural Network based Community Detection using Node Clustering
content.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promising performance across a number of tasks in recent years. Unsupervised community detection using GNNs involves the clustering of nodes of a graph given both the features of nodes as well as the structure of the graph, and has many applications to real world tasks from social networks to genomics. Unfortunately, there has been relatively little research using GNNs for commOunity detection, and even less that evaluates the systems rigorously and fairly. A comprehensive evaluation of the performance of GNNs requires an suitable environment within which they are evaluated. This is exacerbated by the fact that community detection is primarily an unsupervised task, and that (graph) neural networks are used which contain many hyperparameters, discovered by inconsistent procedures. We argue that there is currently a gap in the literature that establishes a sufficient benchmarking environment for the consistent evaluation of GNN based community detection, thereby impeding progress in this nascent field. In this work we propose and evaluate an environment for the consistent evaluation of neural community detection. With this we show the strong dependence of the performance to the experimental settings , thereby motivating the use of this framework to facilitate research into GNN based community detection.
